rv.q: Thomas Ostermeier's legendary Ibsen production is surreal, provocative and very funny.
It is an urgent but tendentious rendering of an ambivalent play.
A play for today, on paper, but the concept could use a digital-era upgrade, and a shot more vigour, to set the world on fire.
We do not need to pay West End prices to be beaten around the head like this.
Ostermeier’s production smashes the fourth wall and gives us some revolutionary theatre.
The whole thing has a contemporaneity that makes it feel urgent, a tribute both to Ibsen’s prescience and to Ostermeier’s rigorous analysis of its relevance.

This Enemy of the People courses with anger to burn, too much of it of the preemptive, predigested sort that pales into significance once you exit the theatre only to land back in the ongoing lacerations of life.

cn.t: Ostermeier's provocative, anarchic Ibsen adaptation divides critics: some hail its surreal, rock 'n' roll energy and humor, while others find it heavy-handed and surprisingly toothless despite its bold approach.
